near_misses.why_not: Same strategy/command class line, but DSN-01 asks for a pattern comment and DSN-06 whether a function value would serve; DSN-01 Limits: 'a pattern realized without a type of its own ... lies outside the rule' and 'the rule asks only for the comment'.
DSN-01 Limits skip 'an accept method taking a ShapeVisitor' (the pattern is named in the declaration); DSN-07 asks whether a checked match should replace the visitor.
Accessor returning a new object vs other routes to a second instance; DSN-04 Limits: 'whether an accessor that builds a new object on every call keeps the pattern ... are outside the rule'.
Same constructor signature; DSN-02 asks for five or more optional inputs taken by position, DSN-17 for a value most call sites pass with no default.
Both dispatch on signal:many_parameters, but CODE-39 asks 'more than five parameters' of any routine and DSN-02 asks about optional inputs taken by position on a constructor or factory.
An upward import can trip both, but DSN-10 asks whether it closes a cycle and DSN-11 whether it breaks a declared direction.
DSN-14 excludes forwarding 'on no object that the routine's own instance holds'; its Limits leave that case to the wrapper rule.
DSN-14 excludes 'overrides of an inherited method' and 'constructors that pass their parameters to a parent's constructor', DSN-16's cases.
DSN-22 counts three or more uses of one string literal within a file; DSN-25 a value copied across files or artifacts.
DSN-24 asks about a hand-written form of a type or schema declaration; DSN-28 about code that parses or builds data another module also encodes.
Same public field line; DSN-30 asks whether its uses need the level, DSN-31 whether the type keeps a condition on the field.
Same protected field line; DSN-31 asks about the invariant, DSN-38 about a subclassable class opening data to subclasses.
`cart._subtotal = 0` can trip both; DSN-31 asks about the type's invariant, DSN-33 about the non-public mark's scope.
DSN-36 flags the subclass's override line, DSN-41 the base class's call or declaration line: two sides of one hazard, never one span.
Same constructor call line; DSN-41 asks whether self-use is documented or the class closed, DSN-42 whether construction calls an overridable method; the conflict is listed under contradictions.
`case "team":` trips both; DSN-08 asks whether one requirement spreads over modules, DSN-47 whether a fixed set is typed as a string.
`status: string` beside optional fields; DSN-47 asks for an enumeration, DSN-49 for a sum type over the case-dependent fields.
A callback that mutates its element parameter; DSN-54 asks about effects in a step function, DSN-64 about an undeclared change to a caller's argument.
API-18 asks about a parameter passed only to receive a result; DSN-64 about an undeclared change to an argument the caller still holds.
`price.setAmount(price.amount().multiply(rate))` trips both; DSN-67 asks whether a shared value is changed in place, DSN-29 whether outside code keeps the type's invariant.
In DSN-72's bad Example DSN-68 flags the DEFAULT_PATHS declaration and DSN-72 the lines that hand it out as a default: different lines.
CHG-29 asks what else a tool-generated change holds; DSN-24 asks whether a marked generated file is edited by hand.

contradictions.sentence_a: A wrapper the project owns around a third-party library other than an RPC client, written so that tests double the wrapper instead of the library, hides that library when the library's low-level API, concepts and exceptions stay inside its boundary
contradictions.sentence_b: A thin wrapper the project owns around a third-party library other than an HTTP or RPC client, stating the operations the code needs in the application's own terms so that unit tests double the wrapper rather than the library's types and integration tests run the wrapper against the real library, meets the material need for a test double.
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: The project-owned wrapper case leaves out an HTTP client as well as an RPC client: tests of such a client run the production client over the real transport against a test server rather than double a wrapper. (TST-06 states the same: 'An HTTP or RPC client is the exception to wrapping'.)

contradictions.sentence_a: When added code repeats a block found elsewhere in the change or in the repository, and the copies are meant to do the same thing, so that a fix or a change of behaviour in one would have to be made in the other, the block is written once as a routine that each place calls.
contradictions.sentence_b: Where calling the routine would make the module depend on a package it is kept free of, a small copy is accepted.
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: A small copy kept so that its module stays free of a dependency, which a stated dependency policy or a comment beside the copy naming the avoided package records, is outside the rule.

contradictions.sentence_a: A declaration widened only so that a test can reach it meets the rule when it carries the project's marker for test-only visibility.
contradictions.sentence_b: A declaration made public, exported or protected only so that a test can reach it, a private-name mark dropped only for a test, and a test-double implementation exported from the production API that consumes its interface break the rule, whatever a comment or an annotation says about who may call it.
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: A declaration widened only so that a test can reach it meets the rule when it carries the project's marker for test-only visibility and reaches no further than the package or module level; a public, exported or protected widening for tests is judged by its own rule.

contradictions.sentence_a: ... a pair of accessors over one of the object's own fields — a getter and a setter method, or a property's get and set — whose bodies do nothing but return that field and assign their argument to it is replaced by the field itself, made public.
contradictions.sentence_b: Outside code changes such a field only through an operation of the type that applies the type's checks and updates. A setter that only assigns the field is not such an operation, since it differs from a public field only in syntax.
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: A pair over a field that the type validates or keeps consistent with other fields in its other operations is outside the rule: there the setter that only assigns is the defect and the field stays private.

contradictions.sentence_a: ... is replaced by the field itself, made public. (good Example: `count = 0;`)
contradictions.sentence_b: A field that is assigned only while its object is constructed or initialized ... is declared with the no-reassignment modifier or annotation its language offers for fields ... and its type has no setter or other method that assigns it afterwards. A setter that no code calls does not change this
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: A pair whose setter no code calls is outside the rule: the field is then assigned only at construction, so the setter goes and the field stays read-only, behind its getter or as a read-only public field.

contradictions.sentence_a: It documents that self-use as an extension contract for subclass authors: the doc-comment of each non-private method that calls an overridable method, directly or through private helpers, or the type's documentation, names the methods it calls and how it calls them
contradictions.sentence_b: A call made on purpose, such as a documented hook the constructor invokes, stays within the rule: none of the cited rules exempts it, and one says not to suppress the warning and to redesign the constructor to eliminate the call.
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: A call that a constructor, initializer, copy or deserialization routine makes on the object under construction is not made acceptable by documenting it; such a call is judged by its own rule.

contradictions.sentence_a: Look for an override that only throws, does nothing, or gives an inherited routine a different effect (Validator), flagged when 'an inherited or gained routine does not apply to it'
contradictions.sentence_b: A base type's documentation may specify some methods as optional and direct an implementation that does not support one to throw an unsupported-operation error, as collection interfaces do; an override that throws there follows the documented contract and is outside the rule.
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: An override that refuses an operation its base type's documentation marks optional, by throwing the unsupported-operation error that documentation directs, keeps the base's contract and is outside the rule.

contradictions.sentence_a: Where two values share one primitive representation but differ in meaning (a distance in miles and a distance in kilometres, a user id and an order id) and can reach the same parameter, field or routine, each meaning is declared as its own type
contradictions.sentence_b: Where it cannot — a serialization format with no encoding for a duration, an API whose clients would otherwise have to implement one language's duration parsing, a separate specification that mandates integer timestamps — an integer or floating-point number whose name includes the unit is the documented form
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: A period or a point in time that an interface cannot carry as a time type, held in a number whose name states its unit, is outside the rule.

contradictions.sentence_a: A step whose inline function exceeds the bound for its language, more than one line or more than 80 characters, the top of the documented range, where the language's inline functions hold a single expression only and more than ten lines of code where they can take a statement block, passes a named function instead.
contradictions.sentence_b: A callback of one line or of a few lines that reads without a comment stays inline: that is the case inline functions are for.
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: Where the language's inline functions hold a single expression only, a callback that spans more than one line or runs past 80 characters is past its bound, whether or not the project's style guide says so.

contradictions.sentence_a: The first is a routine whose whole body is one call passing the routine's own parameters, not counting a receiver it declares among them, to another routine unchanged and in order, with no other argument, ... it is replaced by the routine it calls.
contradictions.sentence_b: When the step supplies more than the function means to take, such as the element's index and the collection beside the element, the step receives a lambda that forwards only the intended arguments, the element and, for a fold, the accumulator with it.
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: A function passed as a callback to a step that supplies more arguments than the function it calls means to take, such as an element's index or the collection, forwards only the intended arguments and stays. (DSN-14's trigger matches `const toInt = (s) => parseInt(s);`, whose replacement `strs.map(parseInt)` is DSN-61's [1, NaN, NaN] case.)

contradictions.sentence_a: A construct the language itself keeps to one instance meets the rule directly: ... a module that holds the shared state in module-level variables rather than in an instance of a type, which the runtime loads once and shares with every importer. (fix: 'or the singleton rewritten as a single-constant enumeration or a module-level value'; Validator: 'Pass ... a module whose shared state lives in module-level variables')
contradictions.sentence_b: A mutable object that two or more otherwise independent components change, or observe another component changing — a collection, registry, cache or singleton held at static, module or package level — lives instead in an instance that each client creates and passes explicitly, as a dependency, to the code that uses it.
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: Module-level variables meet this rule only for state that no otherwise independent components change or observe; moving such shared state into module-level values is no fix this rule offers, and that state is judged by its own rule.

contradictions.sentence_a: A value that each caller must set to match its own runtime environment, such as where its data lives, is hard to give a default in advance and stays required, with no value the module would use in its place.
contradictions.sentence_b: A new input to a published function is added with a default that preserves the old behaviour, and never as a new required parameter
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: On a published interface, a new input whose default keeps the behaviour the routine had before the change is outside the rule; making it required waits for a breaking release.

gaps.concept: domain language: code written in the domain's own business terms (ubiquitous language); the slug's second half and PP 'Domain Languages'. No card states it; the only neighbouring entry under ## design in pending-evidence.md is the 'relation between domain concepts is a named operation' entry, a different claim whose search record lists ubiquitous/vocabulary studies
gaps.source_path: dotnet/docs — docs/architecture/microservices/microservice-ddd-cqrs-patterns/ddd-oriented-microservice.md, § 'Design a DDD-oriented microservice' (opening section, second paragraph); fetched with one curl
gaps.claim: "But the important part is not the patterns themselves, but organizing the code so it is aligned to the business problems, and using the same business terms (ubiquitous language). In addition, DDD approaches should be applied only if you are implementing complex microservices with significant business rules." Checkable against a project glossary or the change description's business terms; official guidance, no measured cost. The DSL sense of PP 'Domain Languages' found no GitHub-hosted source.

Validator: 'Open the file and decide from it whether the type or module is meant to have one instance' and 'For each accessor, overload or variant that the hunk adds or changes, trace every return path, reading the stored field and the other accessors in the file.' — a judgement plus a trace.

Validator: 'open the supertypes its class extends or implements, searching the repository for their declarations, and decide whether a supertype declares a method that the added method overrides or implements, or one it nearly matches' and 'For a supertype method the hunk renames, removes or adds, search the repository for subtypes'.

Validator: 'Open the file, then grep the repository for every assignment to the field (plain, compound or increment, through any receiver) and for every call of each setter or method that assigns it.'

Validator: 'grep the repository for the field's or the attribute's name to find the class that assigns it and the subclasses that read or write it' — a trace of the hierarchy, not one light context question.

Validator skips 'a getter and setter method pair the change does not add or that code outside the change calls' and a pair 'overridden by a subtype's own accessor'; Limits: 'A getter and setter method pair that existing code already calls is outside the rule unless the change rewrites each of those calls'; the fix renames uses 'in any subtype or other code that reads or writes it' — all repository-wide.

Validator: 'open the named function's definition, local or imported, and check whether the step passes any argument beyond those the function means to take' — an imported definition lies outside the file.

The bad Example is a Python ABC ('class Store(ABC):'), two triggers target Python ('\bclass\s+\w+.*\(.*\b(Protocol|ABC)\b', 'metaclass\s*=\s*(abc[.])?ABCMeta'), the Rationale covers 'explicit subclassing, registration', and the Limits never restrict the rule to statically checked code.

Rationale: 'Across 395 releases of 30 open-source systems, speculative generality ... affected 80% of the releases; classes were generally more change-prone while they carried it than while they did not, and its removal had a high effect on change-proneness' — measured cost (DSN-08 and DSN-28 are major on association evidence of the same kind).

Rationale: 'the median change-proneness of the affected classes ... was 43 while they had the smell and 26 while they did not ... the study rates the effect of removing the smell as high on change-proneness' — measured cost for the redefinition form.

Rationale: 'several production outages in multiple typed codebases have been reported as caused by such refactors', and the near-miss case it flags ('a method that was meant to override and never did') is a correctness defect.

trigger_errors.pattern: all four: '\bclass\s+\w+(\s*<[^>]*>)?\s+extends\s+[\w.]+' ⊂ DSN-40's '\bclass\s+\w+(\s*<.*>)?\s+extends\s+[\w.]+'; the Python base-class pattern (larger exclusion list) ⊂ DSN-40's (smaller list); '^\s+\*?([a-z]\w*[.])?[A-Z]\w*\s*(//.*)?$' ⊂ DSN-40's embedded-field pattern; the Deref pattern ⊂ DSN-40's '\bimpl\b[^{]*\bDeref(Mut)?\b[^{]*\bfor\b'
trigger_errors.problem: nested in DSN-40: every dispatch of DSN-39 is a dispatch of DSN-40 (checked with python -c on scratch lines; the only escape is a lone '    Ok', '    None' or '    Self' line, which DSN-40's lookahead excludes). No DSN trigger set fails its own bad Example (DSN-20's [] is the documented always-on class).

summary: All 73 design cards were read in full: 34 deferring pairs are proposed (24 within the domain, 10 with API, CHG and PRF cards), and 12 contradictions each get one Limits sentence, among them the HTTP-client wrapper (DSN-15/19), the test-only widening (DSN-30/35), the trivial accessor pair (DSN-32 against DSN-31 and DSN-65), the documented constructor hook (DSN-41/42) and the forwarding callback (DSN-14/61). Facet findings are dominated by 45 cards that list step review for rules about code rather than about the change; the rest are 4 mechanical-to-semantic check kinds, 2 scope widenings, DSN-12's applies_to and 4 severity calibrations. Every card's triggers match its own bad Example, DSN-39's trigger set is nested in DSN-40's, and the one uncovered concept is domain language, for which an official dotnet/docs page states a checkable claim.
